source_read: PDF, pp. 1139-1148 (all pages); Table 1 (p. 1143) and Table 3 (p. 1145) checked on rendered pages; Table 2 (p. 1144) read from the text layer.

claims.note: The claim correctly attributes to this critique, without data, the worry that a colour result showing MDMA may be taken to mean a pill is safe. 'Without data' is right for that argument; the paper does relay two pieces of behavioural evidence, both second-hand and indirect: a survey of over 1000 UK clubbers about how they would change their use if pill quality got worse or better (intentions about perceived quality, not test results), and a Dutch study (Wijngaart et al., 1997) in which having testing facilities was unrelated to drug and ecstasy use. Neither compares people given kits with people not given them on harm, so the claim's 'no study read compared' stands. Unlike the other critique, this one does not support handing out kits (abstract; conclusion). Paragraph numbers for the p. 1143 anchors (The process of pill testing) were recounted in step 2 against the printed page; their pages and data are unchanged from the blind reading.

anchors.locator: The usefulness of pill testing, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors call false reassurance, an MDMA identification being read as meaning the pill is safe, a particular worry; they give no data on it. Testing also cannot reveal individual metabolic vulnerability.

anchors.locator: The usefulness of pill testing > For harm reduction purposes, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Evidence that testing changes behaviour is described as not substantiated. Relayed: over 1000 UK clubbers asked hypothetically about pill quality (if worse, over 20% would take more, just over a third less, 40% no change; if better, 40% more, just over 10% less, nearly half no change); and a Dutch study in which the presence of testing facilities was unrelated to drug and ecstasy use.

The authors reject kits as protection, say testing at best gives an artificial impression of safety and that knowledge does not always change behaviour, and expect simpler harm-reduction measures to do more; they do not support distributing kits.

anchors.locator: The process of pill testing, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Commercial colour tests do not detect 4-MTA, the reaction for PMA may be unknown, and the makers attach a disclaimer that a result does not indicate safety.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'in all 53 samples with MDMA-like substances and in no others' is exactly what Table 3 shows, but the same table files a separate purple/violet ('opiates') reading in 14 samples with no opiate or MDMA on GC-MS; the 'no others' depends on laboratory staff separating purple/violet from purple/blue/black, a distinction people reading kits themselves may not make. In all, 43 presumptive colour readings (21 amphetamine, 8 2C-B, 14 opiate) had no matching drug on GC-MS.
claims.note: Numbers recompute from Table 3 (Murphy, 1999): purple/blue/black 53, all MDMA-like by GC-MS, and all 53 MDMA-like samples gave it; orange/brown 47 with amphetamines and 21 GC-MS negative; yellow/green 8 and purple/violet 14, all GC-MS negative; no colour 44; the cells sum to 187 for n = 156. Further reporting issues: the text's figure of active drug in 75% of pills analysed (about 117) does not reconcile with the table (100 samples in the listed classes, 64% of 156); the author is Murphy in Table 3, Murphay in the text and reference list (MSc thesis, King's College London, 1999). The blinding sentence is ambiguous: the Marquis test was done before GC-MS 'by laboratory staff who were blind to the initial results', which may mean the GC-MS analysts were blind to the Marquis results or the Marquis readers to the physical description; 'Marquis read by laboratory staff' is a fair reading. The data come from the third author's own unit (St George's Toxicology Unit) and an MSc thesis at the first two authors' institution. For the second-hand sentence: MDMA, MDEA and MDA similar colours, other substances react, more than one drug combines colours and no strength information are all in Winstock; tablet dyes and aspirin and sugar are not (they are in Philp). Paragraph numbers for the p. 1143 anchors (The process of pill testing) were recounted in step 2 against the printed page; their pages and data are unchanged from the blind reading.

anchors.locator: Comparison of the Marquis test with GC-MS analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3
anchors.extracted: 156 samples from an amnesty bin at a large London dance venue, emptied by police and sent to the St George's toxicology laboratory; Marquis test on all pills before GC-MS. Active drug in 75%. The test performed well for MDMA and MDEA (purple/blue/black in all 53 MDMA-like samples and in no other) but gave 21 presumptive amphetamine (orange/brown, against 47 confirmed), 8 presumptive 2C-B (diphenhydramine) and 14 presumptive codeine or dihydrocodeine (purple/violet) results that GC-MS did not confirm; 44 gave no colour. Table cells total 187 for n = 156.

anchors.locator: The process of pill testing, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
anchors.extracted: Marquis colours are hard to describe and subjective; MDMA and MDEA give violet-purple turning blue-black and MDA blue-black, but many other substances react, several with violet (codeine, dihydrocodeine, morphine, diamorphine, buprenorphine, chlorpromazine), so colour tests are non-specific.

anchors.locator: The process of pill testing, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: When more than one drug is present the colour may be a combination of colours; many substances give colours with sulphuric acid alone, which laboratories check for and clubbers cannot.

anchors.locator: The usefulness of pill testing, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Colour tests give no indication of many harmful substances and no information on a pill's strength, and cannot separate optical isomers.

Authors' own ratings, without data: an on-site do-it-yourself colour test is poor for MDMA and DOB, ineffective for 2C-B, 4-MTA and atropine, other contaminants and dosage information, and between ineffective and poor for accuracy in users' hands.

claims.note: Winstock states that no test result guarantees or indicates safety and that colour tests give no strength or dose; these are the authors' statements, as the claim says. Its safety caveat is framed around any result and especially a positive MDMA result taken as safe; there is no separate statement about a negative result, though its points that commercial tests miss 4-MTA and give no indication of many harmful substances carry that meaning for colour tests. Paragraph numbers for the p. 1143 anchors (The process of pill testing) were recounted in step 2 against the printed page; their pages and data are unchanged from the blind reading.

anchors.extracted: Pill testing of any kind does not guarantee safety; colour tests are at best subjective.

anchors.locator: The process of pill testing, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Commercial colour tests miss more dangerous substitutes such as 4-MTA; the reaction of some compounds such as PMA may be unknown; makers state that a result does not indicate safety.

anchors.locator: The usefulness of pill testing, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion
anchors.extracted: Colour tests give no information on a pill's strength; on-site colour tests can confirm neither dose nor precise chemical composition, and a purple/blue/black Marquis colour does not establish that a pill contains MDMA.
